consensus_summary: The blind consensus most frequently identifies the moon as the Church (or believer), which has no light of its own and reflects the light of Christ the Sun, a patristic 'mysterium lunae' reading; strong secondary meanings include eschatological judgment (moon darkened/turned to blood), Israel or a maternal figure (Genesis 37), Mary (Revelation 12), covenant permanence, and the marker of appointed times/seasons.
book_summary: The book identifies the moon as the Son — Christ, the 'faithful witness' — who shines with no light of His own but reflects the Father's light, the light shining in the world's night; it also folds in the moon's role as lesser light ruling the night and marking appointed times. It explicitly flags the common view (church reflecting Christ) as the position it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: Moon = the Church/people of God, a derivative luminary reflecting the light of Christ (the Sun), with judgment-sign and calendar meanings as major contextual alternatives.
book_core_identification: Moon = Christ the Son, the faithful witness who reflects not His own light but the Father's, shining in the darkness of the world's night.
boundary_disagreement: The book retains the structural logic of the consensus (a reflector with no innate light, ruling the night, marking appointed times) but relocates it one level up the chain: instead of Church reflecting Christ, it is the Son reflecting the Father. Passages the consensus reads ecclesially (Ps 89:37 as covenant witness; the 'lesser light' of Genesis 1) are reclassified as Christological.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the moon symbolizes the Church receiving Christ's light; the book says the moon symbolizes Christ Himself receiving the Father's light. The same symbol in the same reflective sense cannot denote both the recipient of Christ's light and Christ as recipient of the Father's light; the book's common-view note shows it consciously rejects and replaces the ecclesial identification rather than refining it.
rationale: Both readings share the reflection schema, but the central referent is replaced: Church → Son. No consensus response or listed alternative identifies the moon as Christ; the closest consensus material (reflected light) is explicitly cited by the book only as the 'commonly taught' view it supersedes. This is replacement of the core identification, not a boundary adjustment, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL in the pure-absence sense because the book directly engages and contradicts the recognized consensus reading.
strongest_objection: The book's chain is textually clever but inferential: Ps 89:37's 'faithful witness in heaven' is grammatically ambiguous (it may be the moon, or a separate witness), and Rev 1:5 calls Christ 'the faithful witness' without any lunar reference; John 1:5 and 5:19 supply the reflected-light theology but never mention the moon. One could also object that the book merely inverts the same reflection metaphor, so the disagreement is typological application rather than true contradiction — but since the symbol's referent (Church vs. Christ) is what is at issue, the identifications remain mutually exclusive.
